name: J02 counterexample - a refused MCP call never reaches the server
about: J02 counterexample - REFUSING the ask, and proving the tool did not run.
WHY THE POSITIVE JOURNEY IS NOT ENOUGH ALONE. That an allowed call runs
cannot distinguish a product that genuinely gates on the permission from
one whose prompt is decorative and whose call dispatches regardless. This
is the other half, and it is the half that makes the approval mean
something.
THE EVIDENCE IS AN ABSENCE, SO IT IS TAKEN WHERE ABSENCE IS MEANINGFUL.
A screen not showing the token proves very little - a slow render, a
scrolled view or a still-streaming row all look the same. The load-bearing
claim is made OUTSIDE the client, against the server's own transcript:
after a refusal it must contain NO `tools/call` entry for this run. The
server records every inbound line, so a dispatch that happened could not
be missing from it.
That check is performed by the correlation step after the run, not by this
scenario, and this file does not pretend the on-screen absence is the
proof. What the scenario establishes is that the ask was drawn, refused
through the client's own binding, and dismissed.
REFUSAL USES THE CLIENT'S OWN BINDING. The retained Prompt declares its
escape key as reject, so Escape selects Reject rather than a key this
scenario invented.
A DIFFERENT ARGUMENT THAN THE POSITIVE JOURNEY. The text is `refused-call`
rather than `daily-use`, so the two runs' transcripts and screens can never
satisfy each other's assertions, and a stale transcript from the approval
run cannot be mistaken for this one's.
THE TOKEN MUST NOT APPEAR. It is asserted absent on screen as a supporting
signal only. Its real weight is that ZULUQUEBEC7731 exists solely in the
server's source: if it were rendered here, the call would have run despite
the refusal, which is the defect this scenario is looking for.
